newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Foreign reinsurers cautious on Brazil's opening.
newsitem.headline: Foreign reinsurers cautious on Brazil's opening.

text.p: A lack of regulations to end the state monopoly in Brazil's reinsurance industry has made foreign firms cautious but has not squashed their interest in the country's huge market.

"Foreigners are interested in Brazil but they are cautious because they do not know what will be the rules of the game," said a spokesman for a large European reinsurer in Brazil, who asked not to be named.

Reinsurance, under which insurers sell part of their premiums to reduce exposure to claims, has become a promising business in Brazil due to high insurance market growth rates after the government imposed its Real anti-inflation plan in 1994.

Analysts said premiums in the domestic reinsurance market are expected to jump to about 3.5 billion reais from the current one billion reais when the regulatory framework is ready within the next two years.
But the pace of foreign investment in the industry will depend on the legal requirements for operating in Brazil, such as the minimum capital required to open a branch here, analysts said.
"If the requirements are too high we will not come," the spokesman said.

The bureaucracy and degree of access of Brazilian insurers to reinsurance abroad may also weigh on a foreign firm's decision to invest in Brazil, said Marcio Coriolano, insurance superintendent at Brazil's Finance Ministry.
Moreover, foreigners are cautious about the future role of the state-owned Brazilian Reinsurance Institute (IRB), which is expected to be privatized within two years.
"They are afraid that the new regulation will not expose IRB to full competition," said Eduardo Cassinelli, manager of J.P. Woods reinsurance intermediates' unit in Brazil.
Some foreign firms might prefer to acquire a stake in IRB rather than come alone to Brazil, if they were allowed to take part in the privatization auction, he said.
Another reason for hesitancy is that foreign firms know little about the Brazilian market and its risks, said Antonio Penteado Mendonca, an insurance consultant.
He said Brazil does not have rating agencies yet to tell the market about the risks attached to Brazilian insurance firms or the quality of their portfolios.

According to forecasts, the Brazilian government should approve the new regulations governing the reinsurance market by mid-1997. "I believe our reinsurance market will be totally opened as of 1998, but this is just a guess," said Paulo Cesar Reis, IRB's director of foreign operations.
Meanwhile, foreign reinsurers already have gotten to work in Brazil. The first move was made by Swiss Reinsurance Co RUKZ.S, which in August opened an office in Sao Paulo to conduct market studies.
Others, such as Muenchener Rueckversicherungs-Gesellschaft or Munich Re, are already planning to open offices in the country, said IRB's commercial superintendant, Walter Polido.
"They are coming now to learn about the market and form their own team of specialists," said Coriolano.
